quality.prompt_text:
Read the following operational notes carefully.

Section 1: Operating a shared inference cluster. Capacity planning starts by separating prefill work from decode work, because the two have different bottlenecks. Prefill is compute bound and scales with the number of prompt tokens multiplied by the model width. Decode is latency bound at small batch sizes and is dominated by per-token weight traffic and kernel launch overhead. A cluster that mixes long prompts with many short chats will therefore show bimodal latency, and the scheduler has to decide whether to chunk a long prefill or to admit more decode steps first. Operators usually pin a maximum batched token count so that one very long request cannot stall every other request. The tradeoff is that chunking a prefill adds first-token latency for that request in exchange for steadier inter-token latency elsewhere.

Section 2: Quantisation for inference. Weight-only quantisation reduces the bytes that must be read for each generated token, which is the main lever for single-stream decode throughput on memory-bandwidth-limited devices. Activation quantisation reduces arithmetic cost but requires careful calibration because outliers in a few channels can dominate the error. Group-wise scales, typically one scale per 128 weights, recover most of the accuracy lost at four bits. The practical question is never only about perplexity: a quantised model must also keep instruction following, refusal behaviour and long-context retrieval intact. Teams therefore keep a small regression suite of prompts and compare outputs against the full-precision checkpoint, treating any change in the answer as a review item rather than an automatic failure.

Section 3: Speculative decoding. A speculative method proposes several future tokens with a cheap model, then verifies them in a single forward pass of the target model. Because verification keeps only tokens that the target would have produced under its own distribution, greedy output is unchanged and sampled output remains statistically identical. The speedup is bounded by two quantities: the acceptance rate of the proposals and the cost of the proposal step itself. Multi-token prediction heads are attractive because they live inside the model checkpoint and add only one small decoder layer, so the proposal cost is a few percent of a full forward pass. The main risk is distribution shift: if the head was trained beside a base model and is later paired with a fine-tuned or post-trained model, acceptance can fall and the expected speedup with it.

Section 4: Attention variants. Full attention keeps a per-token key and value cache, so its memory footprint grows linearly with context length. Linear attention variants replace the growing cache with a fixed-size recurrent state, trading exact retrieval for constant memory. Hybrid stacks interleave the two, for example three linear layers followed by one full-attention layer, to keep most of the efficiency while retaining a mechanism for long-range lookup. Serving such a model requires two different cache layouts in the same engine, and the scheduler must allocate blocks for both. A common mistake is to tune the full-attention cache dtype while forgetting that the recurrent state has its own precision requirement, which is often stricter.

Section 5: Measurement discipline. A latency number is only useful if the protocol that produced it is documented. Report the prompt token count, the generated token count, whether the run was warm, how many repetitions were used, and how outliers were handled. Separate first-token latency from inter-token latency, because a single end-to-end average hides the fact that a long prompt can dominate the wall clock while decode speed is unchanged. Pin clocks or record them, since a boost clock at the start of a run can make the first measurement look better than the steady state. Finally, always report the median and a spread alongside any speedup claim; a ratio computed from two noisy single runs is not evidence.

Section 6: Reliability of multimodal serving. Media inputs arrive in inconsistent formats, with variable frame rates, missing audio tracks, rotation metadata and codecs that decode differently on different hosts. A serving stack should normalise inputs before they reach the model, cache decoded frames by content hash, and cap the number of visual tokens per request so that one oversized clip cannot exhaust the context window. Observability matters as much as throughput: log the number of frames, the number of audio tokens and the prompt length for every request, and treat a sudden change in those distributions as a signal that an upstream client changed its behaviour. Without that, a throughput regression is easily misattributed to the model or the accelerator.
